note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  - Acute wheeze and shortness of breath for 2–3 days. No specific trigger identified in the consultation.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  - Symptoms began 2–3 days ago with cough and subjective fever; progressive exertional breathlessness such that the patient cannot walk to work and sometimes cannot finish a sentence when breathless.
- ENT symptoms:
  - Throat swelling/closure sensation: Not reported.
  - Voice change/hoarseness: Not reported.
  - Dysphagia/odynophagia: Not reported.
  - Drooling: Not reported.
  - Nasal/ocular symptoms: History of hay fever noted; no acute nasal or ocular symptoms described in this episode.
  - Stridor/noisy breathing: Not reported.
  - Dyspnea: Yes — exertional and intermittent at rest; sometimes unable to finish sentences.
  - Distribution of swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face): Not reported.
  - Ear/neck symptoms: Not reported.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  - History of asthma (childhood and adult); described as “quite bad” historically.
  - Prior hospital visits for asthma at times; no ICU admissions.
  - Past eczema and hay fever.
- Allergies and current medications:
  - Allergies: Patient reports no medication allergies.
  - Current/rescue medications: Salbutamol inhaler (dose/route/frequency not documented). Patient reports regular use intermittently (“every few weeks” / “normally take it”) — chronology conflict noted below.
- Social/contextual:
  - Lives with partner.
  - Occupation: Engineer; currently off work or working from home due to symptoms.
  - Non-smoker. Alcohol: ~one glass of wine every 2–3 days.

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution: Not recorded.
- Airway/breathing descriptors:
  - Patient reports wheeze and exertional shortness of breath; occasionally cannot finish a sentence due to breathlessness.
  - No stridor or noisy breathing documented.
- Mental status/associated features:
  - No dizziness or syncope reported.
- Vitals and exam findings:
  - Patient-reported temperature: 37°C (self-measured).
  - Other vitals and physical examination findings: Not recorded.
- Presence of another person with the patient during consult: Not recorded.

Assessment:
- Clinical impression:
  - Acute asthma exacerbation / wheeze flare, possible viral- or allergen-triggered, in a patient with prior asthma and allergic rhinitis.
- Key justifications:
  - Recent 2–3 day history of cough, wheeze and subjective fever with progressive exertional dyspnea; past history of asthma with prior hospital attendance (no ICU).
  - Patient uses salbutamol inhaler as rescue medication.
- Conflict noted:
  - Patient initially stated asthma inhalers were stopped ~3–4 years ago, but later stated he normally takes salbutamol. Both statements are present in the transcript (conflict noted).

Plan:
- Immediate actions taken/advised:
  - Prescribe peak flow meter and spacer (to be collected from pharmacy).
  - Advise increased use of inhaler: suggested 2–4 puffs every 4 hours initially (as per clinician advice).
  - Recommend regular oral/intranasal antihistamine (specific agent/dose not documented); clinician to add guidance to notes and patient to obtain from pharmacy.
- Specific instructions provided to patient:
  - Use inhaler more regularly and use spacer for more effective delivery (pharmacist can demonstrate spacer use when collected).
  - Record peak flow readings first thing in the morning and in the evening once peak flow meter received, and share values at follow-up.
  - Arrange a review in about one week to reassess asthma control and consider additional controller therapy if needed.
- Escalation criteria / red flags (as stated in consult):
  - If you develop a high temperature or your wheezing becomes worse, call the service back straightaway for further advice.
  - If symptoms worsen before the planned review, contact clinician/service promptly (patient was advised to call back if feeling worse).
- Follow-up:
  - Telephone/clinic review in approximately one week to review symptoms and peak flow readings; consideration of additional inhaled therapy as indicated.
  - Pharmacist demonstration of spacer use when collected.
- Emergency contact instructions (exact wording from transcript):
  - “If you get a high temperature or your wheezing is getting worse, you need to call us back straightaway so we can just advise you further.”

document_quality / Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Objective vital signs apart from patient-reported temperature (respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation) not recorded.
  - Formal physical examination of chest/airway not recorded.
  - Peak flow baseline value not available.
  - Specific inhaler names/doses and current frequency not documented (salbutamol listed without dose/route/frequency).
  - No written asthma action plan documented.
  - No record of prior anaphylaxis, epinephrine auto-injector, or prior injection therapy (not documented).
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - Patient statements about inhaler use: initially reported stopping inhaler use 3–4 years ago, later stated regular use of salbutamol (conflict noted).
- Transcript quality:
  - Consult audio/transcript sufficiently clear for core history; some short clarifying exchanges and minor conversational pauses. No major inaudible or noisy segments noted.
